kcet|Chemistry|2009|55||0|0.s:
Hydrolysing a dihalide gives a carbonyl compound, but only when **both** halogens sit on the
same carbon — a geminal (gem) dihalide. The unstable gem-diol formed loses water at once:
CH₃–CHCl₂ + 2NaOH ⇒ [CH₃–CH(OH)₂] ⇒ CH₃CHO + H₂O
So 1,1-dichloroethane gives acetaldehyde ✓
Check the others:
(1) 1-Chloroethane is a monohalide; hydrolysis gives only ethanol.
(2) 1,2-Dichloroethane is a **vicinal** dihalide, one halogen on each carbon. Hydrolysis gives
the stable diol HOCH₂–CH₂OH, ethylene glycol, which does not lose water.
(4) 1,1,1-Trichloroethane has three halogens on one carbon; hydrolysis goes to the acid,
CH₃COOH.
The rule is worth holding: gem-dihalide ⇒ aldehyde or ketone, vic-dihalide ⇒ diol,
trihalide ⇒ carboxylic acid.
∴ 1,1-dichloroethane.

kcet|Chemistry|2009|56||0|0.s:
In water three effects compete, and the observed order is the result of all three.
**Inductive effect** — each methyl pushes electron density onto nitrogen, so on this alone
basicity would rise 3° > 2° > 1° > NH₃.
**Solvation** — the protonated cation is stabilised by hydrogen bonds from water to its N–H
bonds. NH₄⁺ has four such bonds, CH₃NH₃⁺ three, (CH₃)₂NH₂⁺ two, (CH₃)₃NH⁺ only one. On
this alone the order would be exactly reversed.
**Steric hindrance** — three bulky methyls crowd the lone pair and obstruct the proton.
For one and two methyls the inductive effect wins. By the third, poor solvation and steric
crowding together overtake it, so trimethylamine falls back sharply.
The measured order of increasing basicity in water is therefore
NH₃ < (CH₃)₃N < CH₃NH₂ < (CH₃)₂NH
In the **gas phase**, with no solvent, the pure inductive order 3° > 2° > 1° > NH₃ is observed
instead — which is the proof that solvation is responsible.
∴ option (4).

kcet|Chemistry|2009|57||0|0.s:
The iodine value is the mass of iodine absorbed by 100 g of a fat or oil. Iodine adds across
C=C double bonds, so the iodine value is a direct measure of **unsaturation**.
The least unsaturated substance therefore has the lowest iodine value.
Ghee is clarified butterfat — an animal fat, made up mainly of **saturated** fatty acids. That
is why it is solid at room temperature, and its iodine value is only about 26–38.
The three vegetable oils are liquids precisely because their chains are unsaturated, with cis
double bonds that stop the molecules packing closely:
groundnut oil 85–100
sunflower oil 125–145
ginger (a drying oil) higher still
So the state of the substance at room temperature is itself the clue — solid means saturated
means low iodine value.
∴ ghee.

kcet|Chemistry|2009|58||0|0:
Glucose is a **monosaccharide**, the simplest form of carbohydrate, so it needs no digestion
at all. It is absorbed through the wall of the small intestine straight into the bloodstream.
That is why it raises blood sugar almost at once.
Contrast it with starch or sucrose, which must first be broken down by enzymes — a process
taking many minutes.
A diabetic on insulin or other medication can suffer **hypoglycaemia**, a dangerous fall in
blood sugar, with trembling, confusion and eventually loss of consciousness. Glucose taken by
mouth corrects it within a few minutes, which is why it is carried as an emergency measure.
Options (1) and (3) have the effect backwards — glucose raises blood sugar, it does not
reduce it. Option (4) has the right direction but the wrong speed, and the speed is the whole
point.
∴ because glucose increases the blood sugar level almost instantaneously.

kcet|Chemistry|2009|59||0|0.s:
A tripeptide is three amino acids joined in a chain, and the chain has a direction — it runs
from the free –NH₂ end to the free –COOH end. So the order matters, and each position can
be filled independently.
There are 20 choices for the first residue, 20 for the second and 20 for the third, with
repetition allowed (nothing stops the same amino acid appearing twice):
number of tripeptides = 20 × 20 × 20 = 20³ = 8000
The common errors are to treat the residues as indistinguishable, or to forbid repeats, which
would give 20 × 19 × 18 = 6840 — neither matches the chemistry, since a peptide chain is
ordered and residues do repeat.
In general, a peptide of n residues from 20 amino acids has 20ⁿ possibilities, which is why
even a short protein has an astronomical number of possible sequences.
∴ 8000.

kcet|Chemistry|2009|60||0|0.s:
A liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the pressure above it. Raise that external
pressure and a higher temperature is needed before the vapour pressure can match it, so the
boiling point rises.
A pressure cooker is sealed, so the steam cannot escape and the pressure inside builds to
about **2 atmospheres**. At that pressure water boils at roughly **120 °C** instead of 100 °C.
Cooking is a set of chemical reactions, and their rates roughly double for every 10 °C rise, so
an extra 20 °C speeds things up several times over.
So it is the higher **temperature**, not the pressure itself, that cooks the food faster.
(1) is true but irrelevant, (2) is a minor effect, and (3) does not happen at all.
The same principle in reverse explains why water boils at about 90 °C on a high mountain and
food takes longer to cook there.
∴ because water boils at a higher temperature inside the pressure cooker.

kcet|Chemistry|2006|18||0|0:
Liquor ammonia is a concentrated aqueous solution of ammonia gas, and ammonia is very
volatile — it boils at −33 °C.
At room temperature a great deal of dissolved NH₃ escapes into the space above the liquid,
so the bottle is under considerable **pressure**. Solubility of a gas falls as temperature rises,
so a warm bottle holds even more gas in the headspace.
Opening it then sends out a jet of liquid and choking ammonia vapour, which can injure the
eyes and the respiratory tract.
Cooling the bottle first does two things: it lowers the vapour pressure of the ammonia, and it
increases the solubility of NH₃ in the water, pulling gas back into solution. The bottle can
then be opened safely.
(1) is wrong — ammonia is not explosive in this sense; (2) it is alkaline and irritant rather
than corrosive like an acid; (3) it is pungent but not a lachrymator, which is a tear-producer
such as chloropicrin.
∴ because it generates a high vapour pressure.

kcet|Chemistry|2006|19||0|0.s:
In 1962 Neil Bartlett found that platinum hexafluoride oxidises molecular oxygen:
O₂ + PtF₆ ⇒ O₂⁺[PtF₆]⁻
For that to happen PtF₆ must be able to pull an electron off O₂, so it had to overcome
oxygen's first ionisation energy, 1175 kJ mol⁻¹.
Bartlett then noticed that **xenon**'s first ionisation energy is 1170 kJ mol⁻¹ — almost
exactly the same. If PtF₆ could ionise O₂, it should be able to ionise xenon too.
He tried it, and obtained Xe⁺[PtF₆]⁻, the first noble gas compound ever made. The whole of
xenon fluoride chemistry followed.
So the reasoning rested on **comparable ionisation energies**, not on size (1) or
electronegativity (4), and certainly not on both being gases (2), which is true of many
unreactive substances.
∴ because O₂ and Xe have comparable ionisation energies.

kcet|Chemistry|2006|20||0|0:
Magnetic moment rises with the number of unpaired electrons:
μ = √(n(n + 2)) BM
Fill the five d orbitals by Hund's rule — singly first, pairing only when each orbital has one.
3d² ⇒ ↑ ↑ _ _ _ ⇒ n = 2, μ = √8 = 2.83 BM
3d⁵ ⇒ ↑ ↑ ↑ ↑ ↑ ⇒ n = 5, μ = √35 = 5.92 BM
The half-filled d⁵ case is the maximum the 3d series can reach: every orbital holds one
electron and none has yet had to pair.
Beyond d⁵ each further electron must pair with one already present, so the unpaired count
starts to fall again — d⁶ gives 4, d⁷ gives 3, and so on down to zero at d¹⁰.
Mn²⁺ and Fe³⁺ are the common d⁵ ions, and both show this maximum moment of 5.92 BM.
∴ 3d⁵.

kcet|Chemistry|2006|21||0|0.s:
An ion in its **highest** oxidation state has already lost as many electrons as it can. It has no
further electrons available to give away, so it cannot act as a reducing agent.
What it can do is accept electrons and come **down** to a lower, more stable oxidation state —
and a species that accepts electrons is an **oxidising agent**.
The familiar examples all follow this pattern:
Mn in KMnO₄ is +7, the highest manganese reaches, and permanganate is a powerful oxidant,
falling to Mn²⁺.
Cr in K₂Cr₂O₇ is +6, the highest for chromium, and dichromate oxidises, falling to Cr³⁺.
The converse also holds: an ion in its **lowest** oxidation state, such as Fe²⁺ or Sn²⁺, tends
to act as a reducing agent.
∴ an oxidising agent.

kcet|Chemistry|2006|22||0|0.s:
sp³d² uses the **outer** d orbitals (4d for a 3d metal), which happens when the ligand is weak
field and the electrons are left unpaired — a high-spin, outer-orbital complex.
d²sp³ uses the **inner** 3d orbitals, and that requires a strong field ligand to force pairing
first, giving a low-spin, inner-orbital complex.
So look for the weak field ligand. From the spectrochemical series:
F⁻ < H₂O < NH₃ < en < CN⁻
F⁻ is weak; NH₃ is moderately strong; CN⁻ is very strong.
[CoF₆]³⁻ — Co³⁺ is 3d⁶, and with weak-field fluoride the electrons stay as t₂g⁴e₉², leaving no
empty inner 3d orbitals. The cobalt must use 4s, 4p and **4d**, so the hybridisation is sp³d²,
high spin and paramagnetic ✓
The other three all have strong field ligands (NH₃ with Co³⁺, CN⁻ with Fe³⁺) and are d²sp³.
[Cr(NH₃)₆]³⁺ is d²sp³ too, Cr³⁺ being 3d³ with two inner orbitals already free.
∴ [CoF₆]³⁻.

kcet|Chemistry|2006|24||0|0.s:
Bond order = (number of bonding electrons − number of antibonding electrons) / 2.
Fill the molecular orbitals for each species.
N₂ — 14 electrons: 10 bonding, 4 antibonding
bond order = (10 − 4)/2 = **3** ← highest
O₂ — 16 electrons: 10 bonding, 6 antibonding
bond order = (10 − 6)/2 = 2
H₂⁺ — 1 electron, in the bonding σ1s
bond order = (1 − 0)/2 = 0.5
He₂ — 4 electrons: 2 in σ1s bonding, 2 in σ*1s antibonding
bond order = (2 − 2)/2 = **0**, which is why He₂ does not exist and helium is monatomic.
Nitrogen's triple bond is the strongest here at 941 kJ mol⁻¹, and that exceptional strength is
why N₂ is so unreactive and why nitrogen fixation is so difficult.
∴ N₂.
